overview:
In Jain studies, "manuscript citation" refers to the ways in which manuscripts themselves record, transmit, and structure information about the texts they contain, the people who produced and used them, and the lineages that authorized them. It is closely bound up with the practice of writing colophons—paratextual notes typically found at the end of a manuscript or textual unit—which function as a traditional citation system embedded in the material object. In Jain palm-leaf and paper manuscripts, especially from Western India, colophons often provide the title of the work, the name of the author or redactor, the scribe, the patron, the monastic lineage (gaccha), the date, and sometimes the place of copying. These elements together form a rich citation apparatus that allows scholars to reconstruct textual transmission, scribal culture, and networks of patronage.

Historically, Jain teachings were transmitted orally for centuries before being written down, and the shift to manuscript culture brought with it new ways of marking authority and authenticity. In Śvetāmbara traditions, the writing down of scriptures after the Valabhī council in the 5th century CE led to a sustained production of manuscripts, many of which include detailed colophons that cite earlier recensions, teachers, or scriptural collections. Digambara traditions developed their own manuscript cultures and citation practices, often emphasizing chains of teachers and commentators. In both cases, manuscript citation is not merely bibliographic; it is a statement of religious legitimacy, linking a given copy to a recognized textual and monastic lineage.

From a technical perspective, manuscript citation in Jainism operates at several levels. First, there is internal citation within the text, where scriptural passages are quoted and attributed to specific canonical works or authoritative treatises. Second, there is external citation in the colophon, where the manuscript identifies itself and its production context. Third, there is inter-manuscript citation, where one manuscript refers to variants, other copies, or earlier exemplars. Catalogues and modern scholarly editions build on these traditional citation practices, translating colophon data into standardized references that can be used across collections. Projects in prosopography and manuscript studies use colophon citations to map monastic lineages, patronage networks, and the geographical circulation of texts.

In practical terms, a typical Jain colophon may include formulaic phrases in Sanskrit or Prakrit that cite the title and sometimes the genre of the work, followed by the name of the author (if known), the scribe, and the patron, along with a blessing for the reader. These citations are often modular, following recognizable syntactic patterns that can be compared across regions and time periods. They may also record the manuscript’s journey—ownership marks, library names, or notes by later readers—thus extending the citation chain beyond the moment of copying. For historians of Jainism, such manuscript citations are indispensable for dating texts, identifying otherwise unknown authors or mendicants, and understanding how doctrinal debates and sectarian identities were anchored in material texts.

Modern scholarship on Jain manuscript cultures emphasizes that colophons and other citation practices are paratexts situated at the intersection of text and artefact. They are products of scribal activity and social interaction, not neutral bibliographic labels. As such, interpreting manuscript citations requires attention to formulaic language, regional scripts, sectarian terminology, and the broader history of Jain communities. At the same time, contemporary cataloguing and digitization efforts translate these traditional citations into standardized metadata, allowing Jain manuscripts from temple libraries in India and collections in Europe and North America to be studied together. For students and researchers, learning to read and critically use manuscript citations is a foundational skill in Jain textual and historical studies.

Because manuscript citation touches questions of authority and lineage, it should be approached with care. Colophons may omit information, use honorific titles that are difficult to map onto historical individuals, or reflect later sectarian reinterpretations. Variants between manuscripts can signal doctrinal disputes or local practices. For these reasons, serious work with Jain manuscript citations benefits from consultation with qualified scholars, traditional catalogues, and, where possible, living lineage holders who can clarify monastic titles and gaccha affiliations. Manuscript citation thus stands at the crossroads of philology, history, and living tradition, providing a structured yet interpretive window into Jain textual culture.

primary_sources.title: Generic Jain manuscript colophon (Śvetāmbara tradition)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous scribe (example based on common colophon formulas)
primary_sources.original_text: इदं ग्रन्थं सिद्धान्तालापकं श्रीजिनवचनानुगतं समाप्तं। लिखितं श्रीविजयरत्नसूरिणा शिष्येण देवदासेन श्रावकेन। संवत् १७८९ कार्तिके शुक्लपक्षे पञ्चम्यां। सर्वेभ्यो जिनवचनश्रवणपाठकेभ्यः शुभं भवतु।
primary_sources.transliteration: idaṁ granthaṁ siddhāntālāpakaṁ śrī-jina-vacanānugataṁ samāptaṁ. likhitaṁ śrī-vijaya-ratna-sūriṇā śiṣyeṇa devadāsena śrāvakena. saṁvat 1789 kārtike śukla-pakṣe pañcamyāṁ. sarvebhyo jina-vacana-śravaṇa-pāthakebhyaḥ śubhaṁ bhavatu.
primary_sources.translation: This text, the Siddhāntālāpaka, in accordance with the words of the Jina, is completed. It has been written by the lay disciple Devadāsa of the venerable teacher Vijayaratna-sūri. In the year 1789 of the Vikrama era, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika. May there be auspiciousness for all who listen to and recite the words of the Jina.
primary_sources.notes: This example illustrates typical elements of a Jain manuscript colophon used as a citation device: the title of the work (Siddhāntālāpaka), a brief statement of its conformity to Jina’s teaching, the identification of the scribe and his teacher, the dating in a regional era, and a blessing for readers. While the specific names and date here are illustrative, the structure reflects patterns documented in Śvetāmbara manuscript colophons from Western India. Such colophons function as manuscript citations, anchoring the text in a chain of teachers, scribes, patrons, and readers, and providing key data for cataloguing and historical reconstruction.

primary_sources.title: Definition of colophon in Jain manuscript culture
primary_sources.author: Traditional usage summarized in modern description
primary_sources.original_text: ग्रन्थान्ते लिखितं यत् तद् कोलोफोन् इति कथ्यते। तत्र ग्रन्थनाम लेखकः दाता स्वामी पाठकाः च निर्दिश्यन्ते, शुभकामना च क्रियते।
primary_sources.transliteration: granthānte likhitaṁ yat tad kolophon iti kathyate. tatra grantha-nāma, lekhakaḥ, dātā, svāmī, pāthakāḥ ca nirdiśyante, śubha-kāmanā ca kriyate.
primary_sources.translation: What is written at the end of a manuscript is called a colophon. There the name of the text, the scribe, the donor, the owner, and the readers are indicated, and a wish for good fortune is expressed.
primary_sources.notes: This schematic Sanskrit description reflects how Jain manuscript culture understands the function of the colophon. It highlights the citation role of the colophon: naming the text and the key human agents connected to it, and adding a blessing. Modern reference works on Jain manuscripts describe colophons in similar terms, noting that they often include decorative elements and are frequently composed in Sanskrit even when the main text is in Prakrit or Gujarati. As a citation device, the colophon bridges textual authority and social context.

misconceptions.myth: Manuscript citations in Jain colophons are purely decorative and have no scholarly value.
misconceptions.reality: Colophons and other manuscript citations are central sources for reconstructing Jain textual history, monastic lineages, and patronage networks. They provide dates, names of authors and scribes, sectarian affiliations, and information about manuscript circulation. Far from being merely decorative, they are key data points for philology, prosopography, and the study of Jain communities.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain manuscripts follow a single, fixed citation formula in their colophons.
misconceptions.reality: While many Jain colophons share common structural elements, their syntax and content vary by region, period, sect, and even individual scribe. Some emphasize monastic lineage, others patronage or place of copying; some are brief, others elaborate. Comparative study shows modular patterns rather than a single fixed formula, and careful reading is required to interpret each colophon correctly.

misconceptions.myth: If a manuscript colophon does not name an author, the text must be anonymous and historically unknowable.
misconceptions.reality: Absence of an author’s name in a colophon does not automatically render a text anonymous in a strong sense. Authorial attribution may be preserved in other manuscripts, internal citations, commentarial traditions, or later catalogues. Scholars often use multiple manuscript citations and external sources to identify authors or redactors, even when individual colophons are silent on this point.

misconceptions.myth: Modern cataloguing and digital metadata make traditional manuscript citations obsolete for Jain studies.
misconceptions.reality: Modern catalogues and digital projects depend heavily on traditional manuscript citations for their metadata. Titles, authors, dates, and lineage information are usually derived from colophons and other paratexts. Rather than replacing traditional citations, contemporary tools translate and systematize them, making Jain manuscript cultures more accessible while preserving the interpretive challenges inherent in the original sources.
